newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Serb party issues warning, Plavsic lashes out.
newsitem.headline: Serb party issues warning, Plavsic lashes out.

text.p: The Bosnian Serb republic's ruling party on Tuesday warned President Biljana Plavsic she would be ousted unless she obeyed its government, dominated by hardliners obstructing the Bosnian peace process.

The Serb Democratic Party (SDS) leadership said Plavsic should comply or hand over power to Vice-President Dragoljub Mirjanic until the Bosnian Serb parliament, due to meet on Friday, removes her from power.

The SDS, which is covertly led by former President Radovan Karadzic, an indicted war criminal, said Plavsic acted unconstitutionally when she tried to sack the country's police chief in a crackdown on government corruption.
Plavsic was elected president last year when the international community forced Karadzic to renounce public office although it has not been able to prevent him wielding power behind the scenes.
Diplomats said it would be a setback for the fragile peace process if Karadzic succeeded in toppling Plavsic, a wartime hardliner who has since become more pragmatic.
Aware that powerful hardliners would try to oust her, a nervous Plavsic warned at a press conference in her northern industrial base of Banja Luka of the dangers and said:
"There is no budget in the Bosnian Serb republic. The police are smuggling, the people are in misery and the country is isolated."
Plavsic later delivered a similar message in an extraordinary speech broadcast on Serb television, accusing the government of conducting "shameful" smuggling deals authorised by Karadzic.
"The consequence of this is an enormous accumulation of wealth for a relatively small number of our population. Do they think that the rest of the population will be their slaves?" she said.
Plavsic lashed out at Interior Minister Dragan Kijac, who she said was "playing with fire" by refusing to cooperate with international police monitors.
The 40-minute address represented an unprecedented attack on Karadzic's circle on the same television station that glorified his party for the past five years.
Political sources said military officers, some of whom remain loyal to Plavsic, may have secured her TV appearance as the army controls Serb television transmitters.

Relations between Plavsic and the hardliners reached a crisis at the weekend when she tried to dismiss Kijac as interior minister for refusing to investigate suspect companies run by Karadzic and senior official Momcilo Krajisnik.
Although technically the Bosnian Serb head of state, she was briefly held by Yugoslav and Bosnian Serb police on Sunday when she returned early from a visit to London to deal with the dispute.

Plavsic said in her speech that she was systematically excluded from decision-making by hardliners based in Pale outside Sarajevo and denied the cooperation of key government ministers like Kijac, who are loyal to Karadzic.
She said the Serb republic had to recognise who was the legally-elected president. "One small home cannot have two heads of the household," she said, in a clear reference to Karadzic.

The political battle between Serbs pits pragmatists who support some cooperation with international peacemakers against ultra-nationalist diehards opposed to a postwar settlement that has denied Bosnian Serbs the outright independence they fought for.
Under the 1995 Dayton peace agreement engineered by the United States, the Bosnian Serb republic has an uneasy semi-autonomous status in Bosnia alongside a Moslem-Croat Federation based in Sarajevo.

Plavsic warned the hardliners that their defiance of the peace agreement could backfire with "the international community taking the simple way out and forcing the Bosnian Serb republic into a unitary Bosnia, which would be a disaster for us".
She added: "We have to go out into the world and cooperate with the world."
